claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior in HEA nanoparticles is predominantly governed by surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements.
A surface layer enriched in lower-melting-point elements has enhanced atomic mobility.
The enriched surface layer initiates liquid-like behavior below the bulk melting point.
Rapid quenching can produce HEA nanoparticles with minimal initial surface segregation.
Sub-melting-temperature annealing promotes selective surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements.
Local surface enrichment in lower-melting-point elements mediates formation of a liquid-like surface layer before complete particle melting.
Thermal annealing induces atomic diffusion toward the nanoparticle surface.
Lower-melting-point elements preferentially diffuse toward the nanoparticle surface during annealing.
Weaker bonding or higher atomic mobility accounts for preferential surface migration of lower-melting-point elements.
Surface enrichment in lower-melting-point elements reduces the local melting temperature.
Surface premelting facilitates complete particle melting at a lower temperature than in homogeneous nanoparticles.
Segregation-inducing annealing will lower the onset temperature of premelting relative to homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
The lower premelting onset can be observed as a lower-temperature onset in differential scanning calorimetry.
Annealed nanoparticles will exhibit a measurably altered surface composition relative to homogeneous controls.
Homogeneous HEA nanoparticles without induced surface segregation will premelt only near the bulk melting temperature.
The proposed effect applies to HEA nanoparticles containing at least five constituent elements.
The proposed effect applies to nanoparticles with typical diameters below approximately 50 nm.
The proposed effect may not hold in bulk materials.
The proposed effect may not hold when the fraction of lower-melting-point elements is very low.
